# Vendored `gpui-component`

This directory starts from the complete published `gpui-component` 0.7.3 crate. It is vendored so DBFlux can adapt the editor's find/replace panel and the component key bindings to its keyboard-first navigation.

- Upstream: [`gpui-component` 0.7.3 on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/gpui-component/0.7.3), from the crates.io registry archive `gpui-component-0.7.3.crate`.
- License: Apache-2.0; see `LICENSE-APACHE` and the published `Cargo.toml`.
- Archive SHA-256: `465a363235cd4062ef5f0953fc096fc764ed6f53dfbd9f409f669f93ea3b1ff9` (the checksum the crates.io index records for 0.7.3).

## Local patch list

Every local change is listed here with the file it touches and the behaviour it changes.

- `src/input/overlay.rs` and `src/input/search.rs`: when the overlay sync sees the search session close, it returns focus to the editor only if the panel's search or replace field still has focus (`SearchPanel::has_focus`). Upstream refocused the editor unconditionally, which took focus back from wherever it had moved when the session closed after focus left the panel, for example a pane move out of the find panel while a language-feature popover kept the overlay host alive. Closing from inside the panel (Escape, the close button) still returns focus to the editor. The crate's own tests never apply overlay focus (`!cfg!(test)`), so this path has no test here.
- `src/input/search.rs`: `SearchPanel::cycle_focus` calls `cx.propagate()` when the replace row is hidden or the editor is not replaceable, so Tab and Shift+Tab fall through to the next key binding (DBFlux's workspace pane cycle) instead of being consumed with no effect. Upstream kept Tab inside the panel even when it had a single field, which left no keyboard way out of the find panel other than Escape. With the replace row shown, Tab still moves between the search and replace fields. Covered by `tab_in_the_find_panel_cycles_panes_unless_the_replace_row_is_shown` in `crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/code/vim/tests.rs`.
- `src/input/input.rs`, `src/input/textarea.rs` and `src/input/editor.rs`: `Input`, `Textarea` and `Editor` (`src/input/editor.rs`) gain `redacted(bool)`, which marks the element for rendered-frame redaction and withholds the text from the accessibility tree entirely: no node of the AccessKit update carries the value, so neither assistive technology nor the UI-automation bridge (`get_ui_tree`) can read it, and the bridge's `is_redacted` path also blanks anything the element draws. The input itself is unchanged — editing, focus, masking and drawing behave as before. Upstream only suppresses the accessibility value for masked inputs and password content types, which cannot express an editable field whose text must never be exposed. DBFlux uses it for the secret-store value editor (`crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/secret_store/view/editor/view.rs`, on `Editor`), covered by `the_edited_text_reaches_no_node_of_the_accessibility_update` in `crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/secret_store/tests.rs`, which fails against the unpatched element. The find panel is part of the same patch: Find over a selection copies the selection into the panel's search field, so `Input` hands its `redacted` flag to the overlay host (`state.rs`, `overlay.rs`) and `SearchPanel` (`search.rs`) renders its search and replace fields redacted too; searching still works. Covered by `find_over_a_selection_leaves_the_value_out_of_the_tree`. The delta is also kept as `secret-value-redaction.patch`.

What a vendor bump must re-check: the accessibility arm — suppressing the `aria_value` the input writes into its own AccessKit node — is the load-bearing half. Inside DBFlux's value editor the wrapper already marks the subtree `frame_redacted`, so the patch's frame arm is redundant there; the frame arm is kept so a caller that omits a wrapper still gets the bridge-level redaction. The patch stays vendored and is not proposed upstream. A vendor bump must re-check both arms against the refreshed `src/input/input.rs` and re-run the probe above, which fails if either arm regresses on its own.
- `Cargo.toml`: the `[package.metadata.cargo-machete]` `ignored` list adds `log`. CI runs `cargo machete` over the whole directory tree, so it analyses this crate too, and the published crate declares `log` without using it (it logs through `tracing`). Removing the dependency would change the published manifest more than exempting it.
- `src/highlighter/registry.rs` and `src/highlighter/wasm_stub.rs`: `SyntaxColors` gains the slots `field`, `namespace`, `type.alias`, `variable.alias` and `variable.column_alias`, each with its arm in `SyntaxColors::style`. DBFlux's SQL highlight query captures columns, schemas, alias qualifiers, declared table aliases and column aliases under these names, and the palette styles them. Upstream has no slot for them, so the captures fell back to their prefix (`type`, `variable`) or to no style at all. Covered by `sql_captures_give_each_identifier_its_role` in `crates/dbflux_components/src/highlighting.rs` and `syntax_roles_are_styled_in_both_variants` in `crates/dbflux_components/src/theme.rs`.
- `src/highlighter/highlighter.rs`, `src/highlighter/input_adapter.rs` and `src/input/mod.rs`: the editor's highlighter caches style runs per line. The element asks for the visible lines' styles on every paint, including frames where only the caret blinks or the pointer moves, and each request re-ran the highlight query and resolved every capture, about 2 ms for a dense 60-line screen of SQL. `SyntaxHighlighter` gains a public `revision()`, bumped by `update` when the text differs, by `edit_tree` and by `apply_background_tree`, and a public `cached_styles(range, resolver)` that keeps each line's runs for one revision and one theme `Arc` (compared with `Arc::ptr_eq`, and held), matches only the lines it has not seen, one query per contiguous group, and drops everything when the revision or theme changes or past 4096 lines. `TreeSitterInputHighlighter::styles` calls it. On the same screen a repaint takes about 16 µs and a scroll by one to three lines 65 to 150 µs. `src/input/mod.rs` re-exports `SharedHighlightStyleResolver`, which the `gpui-base` trait now takes. Covered by `highlighter_revision_changes_with_the_text_and_only_then` and `cached_styles_color_every_byte_as_a_fresh_match` in `crates/dbflux_components/src/highlighting.rs`.
- `src/input/popovers/completion_menu.rs` and `Cargo.toml`: the completion menu highlights the characters of each label that fuzzy-match the item's `filter_text` (fzf-style, through `fuzzy-matcher`'s skim matcher, case-insensitive), instead of the first `filter_text.len()` characters. DBFlux's SQL completion offers fuzzy matches such as `alarm_message` for `messa`, where a leading-prefix highlight marks the wrong letters. Prefix matches highlight exactly as before. The manifest adds the `fuzzy-matcher` 0.3 dependency the workspace already uses.
- `src/input/popovers/completion_menu.rs`: each completion label takes the syntax highlight style of its `CompletionItemKind` from the active highlight theme (keyword, function, type for structs and classes, namespace for modules, field, `variable.alias` for variables, operator, constant), so a suggestion looks like the token it inserts. Fuzzy-matched letters are bold and keep that color (labels without a kind color take the theme's blue), and the selected row is marked by a background tint alone, so it keeps its colors. An item's `label_details.description` is drawn right-aligned in the muted color, the label truncates with an ellipsis before it, and the description counts toward the longest-row measurement that sizes the menu.
- `src/highlighter/mod.rs` and `src/highlighter/input_adapter.rs`: `input_highlighter_factory` is `pub` instead of `pub(crate)`. DBFlux wraps the tree-sitter factory for SQL editors so a bare schema name (`FROM layer`), which the grammar reads as a table, gets the schema color from the connection's catalog. Behaviour is unchanged for editors that do not install a factory. Covered by `a_table_colored_schema_name_takes_the_schema_color` in `crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/code/schema_highlight.rs`.
- `src/input/popovers/completion_menu.rs`: each completion response shortlists at most 32 rows with the most characters in their labels plus details, measures those rows at their natural width including popover padding, and uses the widest measured row for the menu's explicit content width. A bounded heap keeps candidate storage constant, and expensive layout calls are bounded even when prefix matches contain thousands of tables; all suggestions remain available. The shortlist is a heuristic for proportional fonts, rather than a guarantee of finding the widest row in an arbitrary list. The width is capped by `Lsp::completion_menu.max_width` and the space to the right of the caret. The virtual list measures against its previous viewport width, so relying on intrinsic sizing kept later long suggestions as narrow as an earlier short response. Measurement happens when items change, rather than on every render. DBFlux sets the cap through `apply_completion_menu_width` (`crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/completion_support.rs`): 640 px at the default interface font size, scaled with it and set again on every open editor when the font size changes. The candidate-bound and Unicode/detail tests in this file run locally only: this patched crate is not a workspace member, so `cargo test --workspace` does not run its tests. CI coverage includes `completion_menu_fits_long_labels_and_caps_its_width` in `crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/code/vim/tests.rs`.
- `src/input/popovers/completion_menu.rs` and `src/input/popovers/mod.rs`, `src/input/mod.rs`: a completion row draws its label in the style the active highlight theme gives the item's `CompletionItemKind` (`kind_highlight_capture`, `kind_label_style`, both public through `gpui_component::input`): KEYWORD -> `keyword`; FUNCTION, METHOD, CONSTRUCTOR -> `function`; STRUCT, CLASS, INTERFACE, ENUM -> `type`; MODULE -> `namespace`; FIELD, PROPERTY -> `field`; VARIABLE -> `variable.alias`; OPERATOR -> `operator`; CONSTANT, ENUM_MEMBER -> `constant`. The style's color, weight and italics apply; any other kind (VALUE, TEXT, no kind), or a theme without that capture, keeps the plain style. The selected row keeps the accent foreground. A row also draws `label_details.description` right-aligned in the muted color, and the width shortlist (`width_measurement_candidates`) adds its characters to the label and detail counts, so a long kind word is measured. The fuzzy-match highlight is unchanged. Upstream draws neither. `CompletionMenuOptions::max_width` stays `Pixels`. The unit tests in this file need the standalone crate and run locally only; CI covers the behavior through `completion_menu_width_counts_the_kind_word` (`code/vim/tests.rs`) and `each_mapped_kind_takes_its_color_from_the_active_highlight_theme` / `a_value_or_unmapped_kind_keeps_the_plain_style` (`code/completion_tests/mod.rs`) in `dbflux_ui_document`. In this fork the label styling comes from `syntax_capture_for_kind` instead, matched letters are bold and keep the kind color, the selected row keeps its colors under a background tint, and the description is the fork's right-aligned muted text; `kind_label_style` stays public for the tests.
- `src/input/input.rs`: synchronize overlays under the input's text-style refinement. Completion rows are measured during synchronization, before the input container is laid out; without this scope they used the surrounding UI font rather than the editor's font and spacing, underestimating filtered table labels. Covered by `completion_menu_keeps_table_labels_visible_while_typing` in `crates/dbflux_ui_document/src/code/completion_tests/mod.rs`, which runs in the workspace CI, using typed prefixes and explicit editor letter spacing to make the measurement mismatch observable in headless tests.
- `src/select.rs`: the trigger shows the committed selection's title rather than the item under the list cursor, so moving the cursor through a filtered search does not change the shown value until Enter. While the list is open and has rows but no highlighted row, the first match is highlighted (`highlight_first_match_if_unset`), so Enter picks a match right after a query that went from no matches to some; the list decides the highlight from the rows it last drew, which are none after an empty result. 0.7.3 itself now clears the query and resolves the committed value in the full list on every close, which the 0.6.1 copy patched locally.
- `src/highlighter/highlighter.rs`, `src/highlighter/input_adapter.rs` and `src/highlighter/registry.rs`: `LanguageConfig` gains `statement_separator` (set through `with_statement_separator`, and through `bolt::syntax::Grammar::statement_separator`; DBFlux sets `;` for SQL). When error recovery runs an unfinished statement into the statements after it, the parse holds a separator token under an `ERROR` node. The highlighter then parses each statement of that top-level node on its own (`compute_statement_layers`, on the sync and the background parse paths), and their captures replace the full tree's captures in that range. Upstream colored every statement after a broken one (`left join bronze.;`) from the error-recovered tree, so a valid statement below lost its colors. The main query is held in an `Arc`. Covered by `a_broken_statement_leaves_the_next_statement_colored_as_on_its_own` in `crates/dbflux_components/src/highlighting.rs`.
- `src/theme/system_font.rs`, `src/theme/mono_font.rs` and `src/theme/mod.rs`: the two theme
  font probes can run again, so a platform that installs its system fonts after the first
  window still ends up with the same families it would have named had the fonts been there
  from the start. `theme::init` subscribes to `App::on_fonts_changed` (the `gpui-pre` patch
  `background-system-fonts.patch`) and re-runs `resolve_default_font` and
  `resolve_default_mono_font` with a freshly listed font set; each probe records the family it
  chose, so a later pass revises its own earlier answer and still leaves a family the
  application or a theme file named alone. The font list and the resolved monospace family
  were process-wide `OnceLock`s: a probe that ran before the system fonts arrived poisoned
  both for the rest of the run, and the monospace one also cached its answer while the family
  list was still empty. Both are now a `Mutex<Option<_>>` that the fonts-changed pass clears.
  `resolve_default_font` asks GPUI for the family with `TextSystem::try_resolve_font` instead
  of `resolve_font`: in the window before the system fonts arrive, nothing outside the
  application's own fonts is installed, and `resolve_font` panics when no installed family is
  in GPUI's fallback stack. Naming nothing leaves the theme as it is, and the pass that runs
  when the fonts arrive asks again. With the fonts already installed the probes give exactly
  the answer they gave before, so a run that has its system fonts up front is unaffected.
  The fonts-changed pass logs the pair it settled on at debug level: each probe says nothing
  when it has nothing to correct, so a cold-start log otherwise cannot tell a re-probe that
  kept the families the first pass named from one that never ran.
  This crate's tests cannot run from the DBFlux workspace (`cargo` refuses to test a
  non-member package that has dev-dependencies), so the behaviour is verified by
  `cargo check -p gpui-component` and by hand: on a machine whose `.SystemUIFont` resolves to
  a system family, the theme names that family once the loader finishes.


## Refresh

Retrieve the desired published `.crate` archive into the Cargo registry cache, verify its SHA-256 against the registry checksum in `Cargo.lock` (or the crates.io index for a new version), and stop if it differs. Extract the archive's single versioned root into `vendor/gpui-component/`, retaining its manifest, license, and source files. Keep the root `[patch.crates-io]` entry and resolve the lockfile with Cargo; check the diff against the published archive to identify every local deviation. Run `cargo check -p dbflux_ui_document` and `cargo nextest run -p dbflux_ui_document` after refreshing. A version change requires revalidating every local patch against the new published source.
